query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: An ultrathin, nanostructured oxide coating deposited on the CoCrFeNi alloy surface will enable an adaptive friction interface that releases stress at room temperature and rapidly forms a protective nanocrystalline glaze during high‐temperature sliding, thereby maintaining low friction and ultralow wear rate from RT to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy with a homogeneous FCC structure that shows low friction at RT but suffers increased wear and friction at elevated temperatures due to surface softening and unstable oxide formation.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultrathin, nanostructured oxide coating (for example, one incorporating alumina or a similar high‐temperature stable oxide by physical vapor deposition) on the CoCrFeNi surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed in air over a temperature range from 25 °C (RT) up to 800 °C, under controlled normal loads (e.g., 5–20 N) and sliding speeds typical of prior tribological tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered coating exhibits a nanohierarchical microstructure (with nano-coupled grains and/or nanoprecipitates) that at lower temperatures provides a stress‐relieving interface and at high temperatures facilitates rapid tribo-oxidation to form a continuous, dense nano‐glaze layer.
generation.mechanism: The nanostructured coating acts in two ways: at room temperature, its intrinsic architecture helps dissipate frictional stress without generating damaging wear particles; at high temperatures, its predisposition to controlled oxidation triggers the formation of a fine, stable oxide (glaze) layer that minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear. This dual action maintains the friction coefficient and wear rate at low levels across the full temperature regime.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the uncoated CoCrFeNi, the coated alloy is expected to exhibit a consistently low coefficient of friction (around 0.2–0.3) and ultralow wear rates (on the order of 10⁻⁷ mm³/Nm) from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The uncoated CoCrFeNi alloy, which shows acceptable tribological performance at RT but suffers from increased wear and friction at high temperatures due to insufficient surface protection and thermal softening.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under dry sliding conditions in air, within the temperature range of 25 °C to 800 °C and under moderate load and speed conditions typical of tribotesting machines.
generation.uncertainty: Optimization of the coating’s composition, thickness, and nanostructure is needed to balance room-temperature performance and high-temperature glaze formation. Variability in coating adhesion and scaling to larger components may also affect outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of CoCrFeNi substrates with the ultrathin nanostructured oxide coating deposited via PVD and a control group without any coating. Conduct sliding wear tests in air under identical loading and sliding conditions while varying temperature from RT to 800 °C. Use in-situ tribometry to record the coefficient of friction and wear rates and perform post-test surface characterization (e.g., SEM, EDS, and XRD) to assess glaze layer formation.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature
Wear rate (mm³/Nm) across the temperature range
Surface morphological analysis and oxide/glaze layer thickness
Nanoindentation or hardness measurements of the worn surfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not consistently exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the uncoated controls over the full temperature range, or if the expected adaptive glaze layer does not form under high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

The AlxCoCrFeNi HEA is a widely investigated alloy system [,,,,]. The alloys evolve from a single fcc phase to a single bcc phase with increasing the Al additions. Among them, Al0.3CoCrFeNi HEA is the single solid solution with fcc structure. It is reported that this HEA shows good mechanical properties such as high plasticity, work-hardening ability and cryogenic strength-ductility balance [,]. However, the strength of Al0.3CoCrFeNi HEA at room temperature is relatively low owing to the intrinsic characteristic of fcc structure. For example, its room-temperature yield strength is reported to be in the range of 150–350 MPa [].
